title: Pool Pilot

pool.notes: Gallons drives every dose on the checklist. If this number is wrong, every dose is wrong by the same ratio. surface_sqft is optional; with it, the spring brief can turn 'lowered 18 inches' into an actual dilution estimate. timezone converts the ICO's UTC timestamps to local time -- without it an evening reading is filed under tomorrow. utc_offset_hours is only a fallback for machines with no IANA timezone database; it does not follow DST, so keep timezone set.

equipment.notes: salt_cell_increment_pct is how big one nudge of the cell output is -- the engine never suggests more than one nudge per checklist. cell_output_pct and pump_hours_per_day are where the cell and timer are set RIGHT NOW; the engine reads them to know whether there is any headroom left to ask for. Log a 'Changed cell output' action and the logged value takes over from here.

targets.notes: [low, high]; null on either side means 'no ceiling/floor, don't nag about it'. borates_ppm is a single target, not a band.

why_these.ph: 7.6-7.8 rather than 7.8-8.1. The ICO reads ORP, and ORP tracks the ACTIVE fraction of your chlorine, which collapses as pH rises: roughly 40% of free chlorine is active HOCl at 7.7, but only ~22% at 8.0. Holding a 600 mV floor at pH 8.0+ means running the cell hard to make up for chemistry, not for demand. 7.6-7.8 is also high enough that the cell's own upward pH drift doesn't need acid every week -- targeting 7.4 on a saltwater pool is a treadmill.
why_these.ta_ppm: 60-80 rather than 60-100. Carbonate out-gassing is what drives the pH climb on a saltwater pool, and lower TA means a slower climb and less acid over a season. The usual reason to hold TA high is protecting plaster from etching -- a vinyl liner has no such floor, so there is nothing to buy with the extra 20 ppm.
why_these.cya_ppm: Left at 30-50 on purpose, even though saltwater pools are often run at 70-80. CYA binds chlorine, and an ORP probe only sees what is unbound -- high CYA would push ORP down and make the 600 mV floor unreachable no matter what the cell does. 30-50 is the band that keeps ORP-based control honest.
why_these.salt_ppm: 2800-3200 centers on 3000, which is in-spec for essentially every Jandy cell. Check your cell's manual: if it asks for 3000-3500, move this band up to match it -- a cell run under its own band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
why_these.borates_ppm: 50 ppm is what makes the pH band above hold. Borates are a second buffer working where carbonate alkalinity is weakest, and they are most of the reason pH stops climbing every week.
why_these.fc_ppm: At least 2 ppm. This is the one number where 'low' means the water genuinely is not protected, whatever ORP says -- so it outranks everything else on the list. The ICO does not measure it; a strip does.
why_these.orp_critical_mv: Below this, ORP is low enough that the water may genuinely not be sanitising, and the honest response stops being 'fix the inputs and wait'. The engine will not compute a shock dose from ORP -- that needs a measured free chlorine -- but it will stop being quiet about it and ask for an FC test today.

cadence_days.notes: Days before the app starts asking. These are reminders, not deadlines -- a stale one is a nudge, never an alarm.

chemicals.notes: Strengths matter: a dose computed for 31.45% acid is wrong for 14.5% acid. Change these if you buy something different.

safety_rules: NEVER pour undiluted acid into the skimmer. Acid down the skimmer runs neat through the pump, heater and salt cell and eats them. Dilute it and pour it slowly around the deep end with the pump running.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.
The pump must be RUNNING before anything goes in, and keep running afterwards, so a dose disperses instead of sitting in one corner.

items.title: Test free chlorine today
items.because: ORP is 495 mV, well under the 550 mV mark where the water may genuinely not be sanitising. Free chlorine isn't measured -- the ICO can't read it -- so nobody knows whether that is a real chlorine shortage or just the proxy sagging. pH and Salt are out of band, which depresses ORP on its own, so this may resolve once they are fixed. It is still worth a strip test today rather than assuming.
items.why: ORP is 495 mV, well under the 600 mV floor, but free chlorine itself hasn't been measured -- a high pH and low salt can both drag ORP down even when there's plenty of chlorine in the water. A strip test today tells you whether you actually have a chlorine shortage or just a proxy reading dragged down by the other two.
items.how: Dip a free chlorine test strip in water pulled from elbow-depth, away from the returns, and read the color within the time the bottle specifies. Do this before you decide whether the holding dose of chlorine further down the list is actually needed today.

items.title: Add salt
items.because: Salt is 2,503 ppm, below the 2800-3200 ppm the cell needs. A cell run under its salt band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
items.why: Salt is 2,503 ppm against the 2,800-3,200 ppm band the cell needs to run properly -- below that band the cell makes less chlorine per pass and works harder to do it, which shortens its life.
items.how: With the pump running, walk the perimeter and pour the salt in a thin ring around the deep end a little at a time rather than dumping it in one pile, so it doesn't sit as a heap on the liner. Let it circulate for the next day and brush any spot that hasn't fully dissolved by tomorrow.

dose.label: 74.5 lb of salt (about 1.86 of a 40 lb bag)

items.title: Bring pH down
items.because: pH is 7.95, above the 7.6-7.8 target. TA wasn't measured, so this dose assumes a mid-band buffer -- treat it as a starting point and retest.
items.why: pH is 7.95, above the 7.6-7.8 target -- the higher it sits, the less effective whatever chlorine is in the water becomes, which is part of why ORP is soft too. TA wasn't measured, so this 25 fl oz is a starting-point dose sized on an assumed mid-band buffer -- retest pH once it circulates rather than assuming it landed exactly on target.
items.how: Dilute the acid in a bucket of pool water first, then pour it in slowly around the deep end with the pump running -- never down the skimmer, where it runs concentrated through the pump, heater and cell. Add the acid to the water in the bucket, not the other way around, and stand upwind while you pour.

dose.label: 25 fl oz (3.12 cups) of muriatic acid

items.title: Backwash the filter
items.because: Never logged. The target cadence is every 14 days -- log it once and the clock starts.
items.why: This has never been logged, and the target cadence is every 14 days -- logging it today starts the clock so you know when the next one's due instead of guessing from pressure alone.
items.how: Shut the pump off before you move the multiport valve to backwash, then start the pump and run it until the sight glass runs clear. Switch to rinse for about 30 seconds to resettle the bed, then set the valve back to filter and log today's date.

items.title: If you can't test, add a holding dose
items.because: If you can't test today, 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine raises free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm. That is a holding dose, not a shock: 2 ppm is below what you would swim in, so it cannot over-chlorinate the pool, and it buys a day without pretending to know what the level actually is. Test before adding any more than this. Acid is on today's list too: wait at least 4 hours after the acid before this goes in, and never put them in together.
items.why: If you can't get to the chlorine strip test today, this 0.25 gal is a floor, not a fix -- it raises free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm, enough to hold the water over for a day without guessing at a bigger dose you can't verify. Test as soon as you can and let that number drive whatever comes next, not this holding dose.
items.how: Wait at least 4 hours after you add today's acid before this goes in -- pH and chlorine swing the water hard in opposite directions, and back to back you can't tell what either one actually did. Once that gap has passed, pour it in slowly around the pool with the pump running, and never in the same bucket as anything else.

items.title: Leave the cell alone for now
items.because: ORP is 495 mV, under the at least 600 mV floor -- but pH and Salt are out of band too, and ORP sits downstream of all of it. Fix those first, give the water a full day to circulate, then re-read. Turning the cell up now just means running it harder against the same problem.
items.why: ORP is 495 mV against the 600 mV floor, but it sits downstream of pH and salt, both out of band right now -- pushing the cell harder before those are fixed just runs it against the same problem.
items.how: There's nothing to add here today -- get the pH and salt doses above into the water, give it a full day to circulate, then read ORP again before touching the cell setting.

items.title: The cell is already flat out
items.because: The cell is at 100% (from config.json), running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom left to ask for -- this is not a setting you can turn up. pH and Salt are out of band, and each of those starves the cell in its own way: low salt gives it less to work with, high pH wastes the chlorine it makes, low CYA lets the sun burn it off. Fix those and the same cell will produce more.
items.why: The cell is already at 100% output running 24 hours a day, so there's no headroom left to ask for -- high pH wastes the chlorine it does make, and low salt limits what it can produce in the first place.
items.how: Leave the cell setting where it is today. Once pH and salt land in band and the water's had a day to catch up, that's when there'll be room to consider turning it back down instead of up.

items.title: Leave the pump schedule alone for now
items.because: The pump is running 24 hours a day, which is a lot -- but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water is going through it. With ORP at 495 mV, cutting hours would cut production exactly when you need it. Get ORP comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, and that is the moment to start trimming hours and watching what happens.
items.why: The pump is already running 24 hours a day, and on a saltwater pool that's also the chlorine schedule, since the cell only makes chlorine while water is passing through it -- cutting hours now would cut production right when ORP needs the help.
items.how: Leave the timer as it is for today. Once ORP is comfortably over 600 mV with the cell running below full, that's the point to start trimming hours and watching what it does to ORP.

items.title: Test borates
items.because: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested. The target is 50 ppm; a strip test once a season is enough to know where you are.
items.why: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and have never been tested here -- the target is 50 ppm, and without a number you can't tell if you need to add any or if you're already covered.
items.how: Dip a borate test strip in water pulled away from the returns and compare it to the bottle's color chart. Once a season is enough, so today's reading will hold for a while.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.

checklist.headline: Test chlorine, add salt and acid, and leave the cell and pump schedule alone today
checklist.summary: Today's reading is fresh. pH is high at 7.95, salt is short at 2,503 ppm, and ORP is soft at 495 mV with free chlorine unmeasured. Test chlorine first, add salt and acid separately, keep the required 4-hour gap between acid and any chlorine dose, and leave the cell and pump schedule alone until pH and salt have had a day to settle.

steps.title: Physical prep
steps.detail: Cover off, cleaned and stored. Skim the surface, brush the walls and floor, vacuum out the winter debris. Reinstall the ladder, rails and return fittings.

steps.title: Mechanical start
steps.detail: Reinstall drain plugs, prime the pump, open the valves, start the filter. Run it 24h continuously and watch for leaks and pressure. Do NOT run the salt cell yet.

steps.title: Base sanitization
steps.detail: Water is unstabilized and probably green-ish. Bring chlorine up with liquid chlorine while the pump runs, then keep filtering until the water clears.

steps.title: CYA anchor
steps.detail: Stabilizer goes in BEFORE the salt cell carries the load -- without CYA the sun burns off chlorine faster than the cell can make it. Sock it in the skimmer, never broadcast it on a vinyl liner.

steps.title: Salt addition
steps.detail: Now bring salt into the cell's band. Broadcast into the deep end with the pump running, brush until dissolved, then wait a full circulation before you trust a salt reading.

steps.title: Borate buffer
steps.detail: Last, because it's the expensive one and it locks in a stable pH. Predissolve in a bucket in batches, and retest pH after it has circulated.

recommendations.title: Borates
recommendations.because: Not enough history yet. Only 10 reading(s) over 2 day(s) -- not enough to call a trend yet. Log your acid doses and give it a month of readings, and this can be answered from your own pool rather than from generalities.

recommendations.title: Stabiliser (CYA)
recommendations.because: CYA has not been measured. The ICO does not read it, so it needs a strip test -- and on a saltwater pool it is the number that decides whether the cell can keep up at all.

recommendations.title: Total alkalinity
recommendations.because: TA has not been measured. It is what acid demand actually scales with, so without it every acid dose is computed against an assumed buffer.

steps.title: Take a final reading
steps.detail: The last confirmed reading before it all goes quiet. This is the baseline the spring brief compares against, so it is worth it being a real test rather than a week-old one.

steps.title: Record what the pro did
steps.detail: Which cover went on, whether the water was lowered and by how much, what winterizing chemicals went in, whether the lines were blown. Two minutes now; nobody remembers any of it in April.

steps.title: Note where everything went
steps.detail: The ICO, the salt cell, the baskets, the ladder, the drain plugs. The classic spring morning is spent looking for the drain plugs.

steps.title: Photograph the equipment pad
steps.detail: One picture of the pad with the valves as they were. This is the single most useful thing on the list and the one most often skipped.

steps.title: Note anything for spring
steps.detail: Anything already broken, worn or annoying. It carries straight into the opening wizard instead of being rediscovered.

disclaimer: Every dose here is an estimate from your pool's volume and one measurement. Add, circulate, retest -- never dose twice against the same reading. Chemicals are handled at your own risk; when a number looks wrong, trust the water and retest before you trust this app.
